raw_response:
I've been working this land for 40 years. I know Quzhou's soil — sandy loam, tends to dry out fast between rains. My well gives me control over water, which is everything here. I'm farming alone now, so I don't take on more than I can handle.

Cotton is my backbone. Always has been. I put 6 mu into it. I switched to hybrid seed years ago — the yields are worth the extra cost. I apply fertilizer in two splits: base and topdress. I irrigate five times: before sowing, seedling stage, boll-setting, and twice during boll development when it's driest. Bollworm and aphids are my main enemies — I spray five times through the season, watching carefully. I rotary till in spring because it's faster on my aging back and breaks up the crust well enough.

Chili I put on 3 mu. It brings in decent cash if the market holds. I use improved local varieties I've bought from the county seed station for years. Chili drinks a lot of water and I irrigate six times. I watch carefully for anthracnose and mites — four pesticide passes through the season. Rotary tillage before transplanting.

Mungbean gets the remaining 1.1 mu. It's a light crop — fills a corner of the field and needs little from me. I barely fertilize it since it fixes its own nitrogen. Two irrigations, one pesticide pass. I no-till it to save effort. It's there more to break the cycle and give me a small side income than anything else.
